principles.trigger_context: Any primary action button or interactive element that triggers a mutation or network request
principles.do_this: Debounce tap handlers or immediately disable interactive elements upon first trigger until the asynchronous action resolves
principles.dont_do_this: Allow rapid successive taps to fire duplicate network requests or trigger redundant actions
principles.rule: Debounce all interactive triggers to prevent double submissions from rapid tapping.
principles.why: Rapid double-tapping causes duplicate transactions, double data saves, and severe user frustration.
principles.example: Before: Button fires purchase API on every click. After: Button enters loading state and disables on first click.

principles.trigger_context: Any component handling API errors, network failures, or validation exceptions
principles.do_this: Display contextual toast notifications or inline banners containing human-readable error messages
principles.dont_do_this: Expose raw database exceptions, stack traces, or variable values like undefined directly to the UI
principles.rule: Display human-readable toast notifications for errors instead of raw system output.
principles.why: Raw technical errors confuse users, break visual polish, and erode trust in the application stability.
principles.example: Before: Screen displays 'TypeError: undefined is not a function'. After: Toast displays 'Unable to save changes. Please try again.'

principles.trigger_context: Form inputs, textareas, and chat inputs positioned near the bottom of mobile viewports
principles.do_this: Adjust container padding or scroll the active input into view dynamically when the software keyboard appears
principles.dont_do_this: Let the software keyboard obscure the active input field entirely
principles.rule: Pad or scroll viewports dynamically so the virtual keyboard never obscures active input fields.
principles.why: Obscuring the input field prevents users from seeing what they are typing, leading to input abandonment.
principles.example: Before: Bottom input field is hidden beneath the OS keyboard. After: Form scrolls up automatically to keep the focused input visible.

principles.trigger_context: UI components, text, and icons that dynamically switch between dark and light themes
principles.do_this: Audit all token values across both dark and light modes to maintain WCAG compliant contrast ratios in every state
principles.dont_do_this: Hardcode color values or rely on inversion algorithms that result in unreadable low-contrast text
principles.rule: Verify accessible contrast ratios for all elements across both light and dark theme toggles.
principles.why: Unverified theme switching causes text to blend into backgrounds, rendering the interface completely unreadable.
principles.example: Before: Gray text remains dark gray when switching to dark mode, disappearing into the background. After: Text tokens dynamically switch to light gray for high contrast.

principles.trigger_context: Multi-step workflows, forms, and input screens where a user might navigate backward
principles.do_this: Persist user input state in local storage, route state, or form management stores across navigation events
principles.dont_do_this: Clear input values or unmount state when a user hits the back button
principles.rule: Persist form input state locally so user entries are preserved when navigating backward.
principles.why: Losing typed data upon hitting the back button destroys user effort and causes extreme friction.
principles.example: Before: Hitting back clears all entered form fields. After: Returning to the form restores previously typed inputs from state cache.

caption:
5 things you should be embarrassed to have in your app 🤮🤮

1. Spinning loaders: Use skeleton loaders that match the screen users are waiting for. It looks cleaner and makes loading feel faster.

2. Dark patterns: Don’t hide unsubscribe buttons or use confusing wording to push purchases. Short-term revenue isn’t worth losing user trust.

3. Unresponsive buttons: Every tap should give instant feedback. If something takes longer to process, update the UI first and handle the work in the background when possible.

4. Inconsistent onboarding buttons: Keep your main continue button in the same place throughout onboarding. Users should be able to move through it without thinking about where to tap next.

5. Developer errors shown to users: Your users should NEVER see a 404, 500, stack trace, or backend error. Catch it, log it internally, and show a simple message explaining what they should do next.

principles.do_this: Acknowledge every user tap immediately with visual state changes, executing heavy processes asynchronously in the background.
principles.dont_do_this: Leave the UI frozen or unresponsive during network latency while waiting for server confirmation.
principles.rule: Provide immediate visual state changes upon tap interaction and handle heavy processing asynchronously in the background.
principles.why: Unresponsive interfaces break the illusion of direct manipulation and make the application feel broken or sluggish.
principles.example: Before: Button hangs with no state change for 3 seconds during upload. After: Button instantly transitions to a loading/success state while the upload runs asynchronously.

principles.principle: Consistent Primary Action Placement in Flows
principles.trigger_context: Multi-step onboarding flows, checkout wizards, or sequential form screens
principles.do_this: Anchor the primary continue or advance action button to the exact same screen coordinate across every step of the flow.

principles.trigger_context: Any interface component, button, or container that fetches asynchronous data or submits a network request.
principles.do_this: Provide dedicated visual indicators, skeleton screens, or spinners for all pending asynchronous actions and data loads.
principles.dont_do_this: Leave the interface completely static and unresponsive while network requests or background data fetches are processing.
principles.rule: Display explicit loading states for every async data fetch or user action to prevent perceived unresponsiveness.
principles.why: Without visual feedback during latency spikes, users assume the system froze and will repeatedly tap or abandon the interface.
principles.example: Transforming a button into a spinner state immediately upon tap while network requests resolve.

principles.principle: Inline Form Validation and Error States
principles.trigger_context: Any user input form, multi-step checkout flow, or interactive data submission interface.
principles.do_this: Design explicit, contextual error states with clear recovery instructions directly adjacent to invalid form fields.
principles.dont_do_this: Rely solely on generic, unhelpful system alerts or leave fields unstyled when validation fails.
principles.rule: Provide clear, contextual error states and inline validation messages for every form input failure.
principles.why: Vague or absent error states cause user confusion, form abandonment, and high cognitive load during data entry.
principles.example: Highlighting an invalid email input field with a distinct red border and explanatory text reading 'Please enter a valid email format' below it.

transcript: So, your coding agent is probably doing these two things behind your back that are slowly  killing your app, and you can't see either of them.  I've published over 15 apps with AI, and these two things were caught in almost all of them.  The first one is likely why your app is laggy.  When setting up the server, your coding agent probably built the app to ask the server  for data every few seconds forever.  This is called polling.  This might feel fine during testing, but when users actually try the app, it'll  drain their battery and lower their framerate.  Nowadays, modern backends like SuperBase or Convex can actually push data directly to  your app when it changes.  So make sure your AI is not polling, but rather subscribing to events as they happen.  The second one can explain why your AI actually keeps going in circles and breaking things.  Every time you request a change, most AIs don't actually change it.  Rather, they create a version 2 on top of the broken version 1, just in case anybody  was using it.  This causes your app to be full of broken code that nobody was using anyway.  Now for your future prompts, the AI will get confused between which is the working  version and now go in circles and break things that seem to be working before.  To fix this, just tell it not to use fallbacks or backwards compatibility.  Just replace the old feature and make sure the new one works.  And if you're like me and you're too lazy to type all of that, you can just send  this video to your AI and it'll figure it out.
